newsitem.title: LEBANON: Beirut dealers see t-bill rates falling faster.
newsitem.headline: Beirut dealers see t-bill rates falling faster.

text.p: Beirut treasury bill traders expect the downward trend of interest rates on Lebanese pound-denominated treasury bills to accelerate in the next few weeks with the two-year rates dropping fastest.
Dealers polled by Reuters forecast a drop of 1-1.5 percent by early January in the top-end two-year rates which are now at 21.42 percent.
Three-month, six-month and 12-month rates, currently at 14.44 percent, 16.79 percent and 17.64 percent, would fall more slowly, dealers said.
They also expected the government to introduce a three-year bond in the next few months.

Banque Audi's Lebanese pound Treasurer Nabil Chaya said the installation of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's new government and the central bank's successful management of exceptionally heavy t-bill maturities in October and November opened the way for the Bank to speed up the downward trend of interest rates.
"With the volumes which are coming in for the weekly t-bill subscriptions vis a vis what the government needs, there is ample room to lower rates," Chaya told Reuters.

"New subscriptions have been varying between 500 and 1,000 billion Lebanese pounds a week since early September and I see no slowing in this trend, whereas maturing bills have now fallen to between 200 and 300 billion pounds a week."
Chaya expected rates to continue dropping steadily and to reach 19 percent on the two-year and 16 percent on the one-year bills by early 1997.
Pierre Gaspard, treasurer at Banque Saradar, forecast a drop of 1-1.5 percent in the two-year rate by the beginning of next year.
"I see the average rate on two-year bills coming down to 20 percent. Rates for shorter terms will also drop but at a slower pace," Gaspard told Reuters.
"I expect the drop to be gradual because a very sharp drop could shock the market and have a counter-effect by enticing some investors to close out profitable positions," he said.

Gaspard said for the last three months the market had consistently experienced surpluses in the weekly auctions reaching as high as 306 billion Lebanese pounds in one week, with most of the demand axed to the two-year term.
Subscriptions by foreign institutions were up and he estimated them at five to seven percent of the total.
He expected the positive trend to continue beyond the start of 1997, assuming domestic and regional political stability.
On the introduction of three-year bills, Gaspard said: "In our opinion it is quite imminent, in the next one to three months."
Talal Abou Zaki, forex manager at Bank of Beirut and the Arab Countries, said interest rates policy was dependent on the political situation.
"I think rates will go down in the near future, but how fast and how much depends on the political situation as a whole," he said.
"I think the market can hold two main points on two-year bills. Even if they fall to 20-20.5 percent by mid-January I don't think they will be short of subscriptions," Abou Zaki said.

"The best European rates are about eight percent on the Spanish peseta and the Italian lira. So 14-20 percent on Lebanese bills is a good yield compared with rates on other currencies, especially European."
